query: For automotive exhaust catalysts, what single intervention could improve catalytic activity and durability while reducing platinum-group-metal consumption? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, defines the conditions under which it should hold, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment with a clear outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Automotive exhaust catalysts that incorporate a high‐entropy oxide spinel support to atomically disperse trace amounts of platinum‐group metals (PGMs) will exhibit improved catalytic activity and enhanced durability while reducing overall PGM consumption relative to conventional supported catalysts. This improvement is achieved via multicomponent mixing, which stabilizes the single-atom distribution of PGMs and optimizes the binding of key reaction intermediates.
generation.material_initial_state: Conventional automotive exhaust catalysts using PGMs (e.g., Pt/CeO2 or Pt/γ-Al2O3) that rely on nanoparticle ensembles with relatively high PGM loadings.
generation.intervention: Replace standard catalyst supports with a deliberately engineered high‐entropy oxide spinel support that has a disordered, multi‐metal composition designed to promote the formation of isolated PGM sites (i.e., single-atom distribution).
generation.conditions: Under realistic automotive exhaust environments, including oxidative atmospheres with cyclic moderate temperatures, and in the presence of water vapor and other exhaust pollutants.
generation.structural_mediator: The high-entropy oxide support’s configurational disorder and oxygen-vacancy-rich spinel structure help stabilize individual PGM atoms, preventing agglomeration and allowing optimal exposure of active sites.
generation.mechanism: Increased configurational disorder in the high-entropy oxide (a result of multicomponent mixing) modifies the electronic structure at the interface, enhances oxygen mobility, and creates abundant oxygen vacancies. This leads to stronger synergistic interactions with isolated PGM atoms, optimizing binding energies for key intermediates in CO oxidation and related reactions, thereby lowering activation barriers and suppressing catalyst deactivation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to conventional catalysts, the intervention is expected to lower the light‐off temperature (e.g., T10 for CO oxidation) and exhibit slower activity loss over time, all while achieving comparable or enhanced catalytic performance with reduced PGM loading.
generation.baseline: Conventional automotive exhaust catalysts based on Pt nanoparticles on traditional supports (e.g., Pt/CeO2) with higher PGM consumption.
generation.boundary: The effect is expected to hold under typical exhaust thermal and chemical conditions; however, stability may be challenged at excessively high temperatures (above ~500 °C) or in cases where the high-entropy support’s phase homogeneity is compromised.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of activity improvement and PGM reduction is uncertain, as catalytic performance may depend strongly on synthesis reproducibility and precise operational conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of automotive exhaust catalyst samples: one set using conventional PGM catalysts on standard supports (e.g., Pt/CeO2) and another set where the catalyst employs the high-entropy oxide spinel support for single-atom dispersion of the same minimal PGM loading. Subject both samples to accelerated aging and exhaust simulation tests with controlled temperature cycles and pollutant flows.
measurements: Light-off temperature (e.g., T10 for CO oxidation)
Turnover frequency (TOF) and overall conversion efficiency under standard test conditions
Durability metrics such as performance retention after extended operation
Microscopic characterization (e.g., TEM/HAADF-STEM) to verify PGM dispersion and stability
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the high-entropy oxide-supported catalysts do not demonstrate significantly lower light-off temperatures, improved TOF/durability, and evidence of isolated PGM sites compared to the conventional catalyst under identical testing conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Increasing configurational disorder demonstrated significant improvements to the catalytic performance of spinel oxides for CO oxidation under dry, lean conditions (excess O2). The 7‐metal HESO demonstrated the best catalytic activity with a 10% CO conversion temperature (T10) of 168 °C, which was a 63% decrease compared to the 4‐metal MESO (at 454 °C). The 7‐metal HESO also showed better long‐term stability than the 4‐metal MESO (4.7% versus 12.2% activity decrease during 14 h of operation) indicating that incorporating more metals could help improve the catalysts’ resistance to deactivation. A series of spinel oxides with increasing disorder was synthesized via a molecular precursor approach which required lower thermal energy input (900 °C for 4 h) than traditional solid‐state methods. Spinel oxide powders with the Fd‐3m (227) space group were comprehensively characterized via pXRD, atomic resolution HAADF‐STEM, SEM‐EDS and STEM‐EDS to confirm the homogenous distribution of elements across different length scales. The catalytic performance of Pd1@HEFO is comparable to Pt/CeO2–SiAlOx regarded as a candidate of diesel oxidation catalyst (DOC) and Pt/CeO2. Moreover, no obvious deactivation of CO, C3H6, and NO oxidation can be observed over Pd1@HEFO even after 10 h of reaction in Supplementary Fig. 14b, implying that Pd1@HEFO shows a good DOC activity and stability. PXRD patterns of Pd1@HEFO treated in H2 at different temperatures (Supplementary Fig. 15) suggest that Pd atoms in Pd1@HEFO are not stable in reductive atmosphere. As a result, our Pd1@HEFO is more suitable for the oxidation reaction under the oxygen-rich conditions, such as catalytic destruction of pollutions emitted from diesel engines. These illustrate that our Pd1@HEFO possesses not only outstanding low-temperature CO oxidation activity but also excellent resistance to hydrothermal degradation as a candidate of DOC, thus possibly tolerating the harsh conditions during exhaust treatment of diesel engines.
